item.title: Cross-Bond Panel Learning for Next-Day Price Forecasting of Chinese Convertible Bonds: A Reality Check
item.description: arXiv:2610.33453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in financial machine learning have prompted growing interest in applying deep neural networks to convertible bond valuation and forecasting. However, existing studies often focus on in-sample valuation fit or cross-sectional return rankings, leaving out-of-sample next-day price forecasting insufficiently benchmarked against persistence. This paper provides a comprehensive empirical reality check on cross-bond panel learning for Chinese convertible bonds. Using a daily panel of 73,806 observations across 100 A-share convertible bonds from 2022 to 2025, we evaluate whether cross-bond neural architectures reliably outperform the random walk under strict temporal splitting, boundary purging, fold-specific preprocessing, and dependence-aware inference. On the 29,514-observation holdout, the random walk achieves an RMSE of 2.3577 CNY. Five-seed ensembles of small and large price-change MLPs yield RMSEs of 2.3619 and 2.3645 CNY, with negative out-of-sample R^2 values (-0.0035 and -0.0057) and target-date clustered HAC p-values of 0.453 and 0.248. Ten-day circular block-bootstrap intervals span zero, while direct price-level training degrades performance substantially. Although cross-bond pooling provides a variance-stabilizing shrinkage effect over single-bond estimation (lowering test RMSE for 79 of 90 individual bonds), it fails to produce an aggregate forecast advantage over persistence. Error decomposition reveals that failure is not uniform: five highly volatile, clause-sensitive bonds account for 74.4% of the model's total excess squared error. Without contemporaneous equity market information or explicit contractual event conditioning, deep panel architectures do not deliver incremental next-day predictability over persistence.
item.dc:creator: Derun Zhong, Guolian Wang, Shiqing Wang, Hongjie Feng

item.title: Det-MASO: Diversity-Regularized Multi-Agent Sequential Optimization for Factor Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantitative investment requires alpha factors that are both predictive and diverse. However, existing factor generation methods, including formulaic mining and neural end-to-end models, are mostly based on a single-agent design, which limits exploration of the factor space and reduces adaptability to changing markets. Multi-agent approaches can broaden exploration, but agents trained under a shared objective often collapse to similar outputs, while existing diversity techniques either scale poorly with asset-universe size or address redundancy only after training. We propose a multi-agent sequential optimization (Det-MASO) framework for generating diversified, context-adaptive alpha factors. It introduces a differentiable log-determinant penalty on the inter-agent correlation matrix directly into the joint objective, discouraging correlated agent behavior during training with computational cost that scales linearly with the number of assets. We further show that this penalty prevents homogeneous equilibria and preserves factor diversity throughout optimization, while a context-conditioned scheduler dynamically adjusts agent emphasis across market regimes and Shapley interaction index analysis is used to characterize the cooperation structure that emerges among them. Experiments show that Det-MASO outperforms baselines, improving the information coefficient by 1.1\%, the annualized return by 6.4\%, and the Sharpe ratio by 0.33.
item.dc:creator: Tiantian Wu, Peng Yang

item.title: Scenario Matching for Credit Dependence Stress Tests: Temporal correlation constraints and empirical risk bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.35118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We couple two sets of simulated market and credit paths by minimizing absolute temporal-correlation error relative to a prescribed target. Each market path receives exactly one credit path, preserving both empirical distributions of complete scenarios. A perfect-matching test identifies whether a uniform correlation-error tolerance is feasible and determines its smallest attainable value. Further assignments give exact empirical mean-loss and exceedance-probability bounds; quantile bounds follow by binary search over eligible loss thresholds. A synthetic bond-forward credit stress test illustrates the method. The experiments report matching precision, empirical score tails and exposure-grid error, and measure matching and mean-loss computation. The method is independent of the scenario generator and provides a reproducible way to examine dependence assumptions in existing risk engines. Tail measures concern default-probability-weighted credit scores. Accompanying reproducibility package (Python code, synthetic scenario libraries, permutations, and benchmarks) is attached in the ZIP archive.
item.dc:creator: Naoufal Nifa

item.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
item.description: arXiv:2610.33122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.
item.dc:creator: Bartosz Ziollko, Adam Niedzialkowski, Bartosz Szyma

item.title: Tokenised Sukuk: A Verifiable Architecture for Asset Evidence and Programmable Shariah Compliance
item.description: arXiv:2610.33538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Security-token standards such as ERC-3643 decide who may hold a token, not what stands behind it. For a sukuk this gap matters: whether a certificate may trade at a negotiated price depends on what its portfolio contains, and a token that checks only investor identity keeps trading after every non-debt asset has been sold. We ask whether this tradability condition can be enforced on-chain, and at what cost. We encode the tradability conditions of the 2023 resolution of the Shariah Advisory Council of the Securities Commission Malaysia on Sukuk Wakalah bi al-Istithmar as issuance and transfer policies that read EIP-712 claims, signed by separate institutional roles, about each asset's rights, valuation, encumbrance and Shariah classification and about the allocation of proceeds. Across 26 scenarios that we constructed on a synthetic instrument, an identity-only baseline wrongly allowed 13 operations that the encoded policy denies, and asset evidence without the Shariah rule still allowed 6. The full policy matched every expected outcome and added 35,834 gas (71.0%) per transfer, independent of portfolio size. Our evaluation also exposes a trade-off that the constructed scenarios had missed. Checking the continuing condition through a single nominated asset keeps the cost of a transfer constant but can block trades the ruling allows, and a bounded fallback scan narrows this gap at about 12,050 gas per scanned asset. Our results indicate that Shariah tradability conditions can be enforced on-chain against attributable asset evidence, and that the way a ruling is encoded shapes which lawful trades a token permits. GitHub repo: https://github.com/rischanlab/tokenized_sukuk
item.dc:creator: Rischan Mafrur, Khadijah, Gun Gun Febrianza

item.title: Fourier-Laplace transforms in polynomial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck volatility models
item.description: arXiv:2405.02170v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the Fourier-Laplace transforms of a broad class of polynomial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) volatility models, including the well-known Stein-Stein, Sch\"obel-Zhu, one-factor Bergomi, and the recently introduced quintic OU models motivated by the SPX-VIX joint calibration problem. We show the connection between the joint Fourier-Laplace functional of the log-price and the integrated variance, and the solution of an infinite-dimensional system of Riccati equations. Next, under some non-vanishing conditions on the Fourier-Laplace transforms, we establish an existence result for such Riccati equations and show how the Fourier-Laplace functional can be seen as the limit of a sequence of entire functions. On the practical side, we develop a numerical scheme to solve the stiff infinite-dimensional system of Riccati equations and demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of the scheme for pricing SPX options and volatility swaps using Fourier and Laplace inversions, with specific examples of the quintic OU and the one-factor Bergomi models and their calibration to real market data.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Abi Jaber (Xiaoyuan), Shaun (Xiaoyuan), Li, Xuyang Lin

item.title: LiveOption: Evaluating LLM Agents in Structured Option Trading with Nonlinear Payoffs
item.description: arXiv:2609.33470v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and multi-agent systems (MAS) have shown promise in financial decision-making, yet existing evaluations focus on equity trading and primarily assess directional prediction, overlooking the structural complexity of derivative markets. Option trading introduces fundamentally different challenges, including nonlinear payoffs and multi-leg strategy construction, requiring structured decisions rather than simple directional bets. We introduce LiveOption, an evaluation framework for LLM-based agents in option trading. LiveOption formulates the problem as structured sequential decision-making under realistic execution and capital constraints, and provides a reproducible environment with standardized interaction protocols. The framework includes three task suites covering portfolio overlays, event-driven earnings trading, and 0DTE intraday trading. We further propose a hierarchical metric suite that evaluates action validity, decision quality, risk characteristics, and outcome-level performance. Experiments show that current agents often fail to achieve competitive returns in most scenarios. LiveOption offers a principled testbed for evaluating structured decision-making beyond outcome-based metrics. Project Website: https://liveoption.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Haochen Luo, Yifan Li, Binh Minh An, Xiaolong Luo, Zhengzhao Lai, Yuan Zhang, Chen Liu

item.title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.35744v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating finance research agents requires rubrics that reflect expert standards and fix the values correct as of an information cutoff. Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. This expert guidance governs every agent, as prompts and as rules that code enforces, and a Task Bank of reusable criteria carries it across tasks. In long-horizon loops that follow the expert guidance, a writer agent researches every expected value and a reviewer agent verifies it, and failures escalate to a human. On three expert-authored finance benchmarks, its rubrics track expert scoring as closely as the strongest evaluated generator while stating the expert rubric's expected value for more criteria, their scores agree with human grading, and in-house analysts prefer them in a blind review. The released 100-query FinAutoRubric Benchmark, built from in-house analysts' key questions across 78 tasks and eight asset classes, shows that rubrics from an earlier model generation still leave headroom for a later one.
item.dc:creator: Hoyoung Lee, Suyeol Yun, Jack Haverty, Yunju Cho, Meesong Kim, Daekyung Park, Sumin Kim, Jihoon Kwon, Jasmine Jia Geng, Andrew Chin, Yin Luo, Edward Tong, Yu Yu, Zach Golkhou, Minkyu Kim, Igor Halperin, Young Cha, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Chanyeol Choi, Yongjae Lee

item.title: Combinatorial Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.23517v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a framework to identify and quantify arbitrage across logically related prediction-market contracts. We prove that prices outside the convex hull of admissible payoff vectors admit arbitrage and identify optimal arbitrage portfolios through integer programming. Using venue metadata and semantic analysis of resolution criteria, we recover 1.9 million logical relations and compile them into constraint systems covering more than 255,000 contracts. We replay full-depth Polymarket order books to simulate an arbitrageur executing these portfolios against resting orders. Among settled portfolios, an ideal arbitrageur that takes the full displayed depth of every opportunity and reuses its capital at resolution earns a risk-free return of 3.5% a week after spreads and fees. We find that arbitrage opportunities persist longer and attract less observed participation where relation discovery and execution are more costly.
item.dc:creator: Hongjian Shi, Daojing Zhai
